newsitem.title: USA: US bank regulators to issue revised insurance rule.
newsitem.headline: US bank regulators to issue revised insurance rule.

text.p: U.S. bank regulators said they will issue revisions on Friday to rules governing sales of credit life insurance by national banks.

Changes to the longstanding rules will direct employees of national banks to base sales' recommendations on whether customers will benefit from credit life insurance, rather than on how much revenue will be generated from commissions.

"If national banks are going to sell insurance, we want them to do it right," said Eugene Ludwig, comptroller of the currency. "That means credit life insurance sales should be based upon customer needs." The changes take effect Dec. 31.

The Office of the Comptroller of the Currency, which said the final rule will be published in the Federal Register on Friday, has been revising various rules during the past year and a half as part of a broad review of its regulations.

The revisions to the credit life insurance rules will also give banks more leeway in how they pay bonuses and commissions. Banks will be permitted to make those payments at any time, rather than be limited to making quarterly payments.
The changes will also clarify when the rule will apply to bank employees who also are employed by a third party.
Bank employees, officers, directors or principal shareholders who are also employees of a separate company generally are covered by the rule unless certain conditions are met.
Bank shareholders with an ownership interest of 10 percent or more will be subject to the rule's restrictions.

Previously, the threshold had been five percent. That change makes the standard for determining principal shareholders consistent with the standard used in other regulations, the comptroller's office said.
